note.text:
Creative Commons (CC) licences let creators share their work while keeping some rights. Others may use it if they follow the conditions:
• BY (Attribution): give credit to the creator. • SA (ShareAlike): share new works under the same licence.
• NC (NonCommercial): no use to make money. • ND (NoDerivatives): no changes; share only as it is.
Licences combine these, e.g. CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC-ND. CC0 means 'no rights reserved' (public domain).
Many images on Wikipedia and many free educational resources use CC licences.

sections.heading: Sharing with conditions
sections.text:
Normally, copyright means 'all rights reserved': you need permission to reuse a work. Creative Commons (CC) licences let creators say in advance 'you may use this, if…'.
This makes it easy for teachers, students and artists to share and reuse legally.

sections.heading: The building blocks
sections.text:
• BY (Attribution): give credit to the creator.
• SA (ShareAlike): if you adapt it, share your version under the same licence.
• NC (NonCommercial): do not use it to make money.
• ND (NoDerivatives): share it only as it is; no changes.
They combine: CC BY, CC BY-SA, CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-ND, CC BY-NC-ND (the strictest).

sections.heading: Public domain and practice
sections.text:
{'CC0'} means 'no rights reserved': the creator gives the work to the public domain for any use.
When you use a CC work, write the title, creator, source and licence, e.g. 'Photo: Mount Cameroon by A. Tabe, CC BY-SA, Wikimedia Commons'.
Check the conditions before changing a work or using it for business.

key_words.meaning: licences that let creators share work with conditions

examples: CC BY: any use with credit

mistake.wrong: A CC licence means you can do anything without credit
mistake.right: Most CC licences require credit (BY) and may forbid changes or sale
mistake.why: Always read the letters of the licence.

worked_example.problem: A photo is licensed CC BY-NC. Can a school use it on a free poster? Can a shop use it in a paid advert?
steps: BY: give credit to the photographer.
The free school poster is allowed with credit; the shop's paid advert is not allowed without permission.
worked_example.answer: School poster: yes, with credit; shop advert: no

cards.idea: NC: no commercial use; ND: no changes; SA: share alike.
example: CC BY-NC-ND is the strictest combination.

pick.q: Using a CC BY-ND photo, with credit, unchanged, in a school magazine
w: No, CC works can never be used
Only if you change the photo
e: CC licences allow use under conditions.
pick.y: Credit given and no changes: allowed.

pick.q: Cropping and colouring a CC BY-ND drawing for a poster
w: Yes, if you do not give credit
Yes, if the poster is pink
e: Credit is still required, and changes are still forbidden.

pick.q: Selling T-shirts printed with a CC BY-NC image
e: Credit does not remove the NC condition.
